subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a relaxed muscle, the myosin-binding sites on actin are blocked by:
options: Tropomyosin held in place by troponin
Myosin heads
ATP molecules
Calcium ions
questions.explain: At rest, tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin, with troponin holding it there until calcium ions arrive.

questions.q: Agglutination by antibodies helps destroy pathogens because:
options: Each antibody has two binding sites, so it clumps pathogens together, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf
It neutralises bacterial toxins by hydrolysis
It directly lyses the bacterial cell wall
It marks the antibody for destruction
questions.explain: With two binding sites an antibody can link several pathogens into clumps that phagocytes engulf more efficiently.

questions.q: Ringing experiments, in which a ring of bark (and phloem) is removed from a tree trunk, support the role of phloem in translocation because:
options: Sugars accumulate in the bulge above the ring while tissues below may die
The leaves immediately wilt
Water stops reaching the leaves above the ring
The xylem also stops functioning
questions.explain: Sugars cannot pass the removed phloem, so they build up above the ring, showing phloem carries organic solutes.

questions.q: Saltatory conduction in myelinated neurones speeds transmission because:
options: The action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier where depolarisation occurs
The axon diameter is reduced by the myelin
Myelin actively pumps sodium along the axon
Myelin increases the membrane's permeability to sodium
questions.explain: Depolarisation only occurs at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, greatly increasing speed.

questions.q: Receiving an injection of antibodies (e.g. anti-tetanus serum) provides:
options: Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
questions.explain: Ready-made antibodies are introduced artificially without the body making its own, giving immediate but short-lived (passive) protection.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes differs from type 2 in that:
options: Type 1 has a later onset and is linked to obesity
Type 1 is caused by target cells losing responsiveness to insulin
Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells so little or no insulin is produced
Type 1 is usually treated by diet and exercise alone
questions.explain: In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells, whereas type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity of target cells.

questions.q: In bony fish, the operculum contributes to gas exchange by:
options: Filtering food particles from the water
Maintaining a near-continuous flow of water over the gills
Pumping blood through the gill lamellae
Adding oxygen to the water before it reaches the gills
questions.explain: Coordinated movements of the buccal cavity and operculum keep water flowing over the gills almost continuously, maintaining exchange.

questions.q: Which type of white blood cell is a non-specific phagocyte that engulfs pathogens?
options: B-lymphocyte
Neutrophil
Plasma cell
T-helper cell
questions.explain: Neutrophils are phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogens non-specifically as part of the innate immune response.

questions.q: In the cohesion-tension theory of water transport, water moves up the xylem because:
options: Active transport pumps water from root to leaf
Root pressure alone is sufficient in tall trees
Transpiration creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules pulls a continuous column upward
Osmosis pushes water from the leaves down to the roots
questions.explain: Evaporation from leaves lowers pressure, and hydrogen-bonded cohesion lets a continuous water column be pulled up under tension.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as HIV?
options: Viruses have thicker cell walls
Antibiotics only work on fungi
Viruses are too large to be affected
Viruses lack the metabolic processes and structures (e.g. cell walls, ribosomes) that antibiotics target
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; viruses use host-cell machinery and lack these targets, so antibiotics do not affect them.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are described as 'monoclonal' because they are:
options: A mixture of antibodies against several antigens
Produced by many different B-cells
Identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells, all specific to one antigen
Made only inside the human body
questions.explain: They are derived from one B-cell clone, so every antibody is identical and binds the same specific antigen.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Carbaminohaemoglobin
Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
Carbonic acid in the plasma
Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: A desert mammal that produces very concentrated urine is likely to have:
options: A long loop of Henle, allowing a steep medullary solute gradient
A glomerulus that filters very little blood
A very short loop of Henle
No collecting ducts
questions.explain: A long loop of Henle generates a stronger medullary concentration gradient, enabling more water reabsorption and highly concentrated urine.

questions.q: Some antibodies act as antitoxins. This means they:
options: Lyse bacterial cell walls
Cause clumping of pathogens
Bind to and neutralise toxins released by pathogens
Mark pathogens for phagocytosis
questions.explain: Antitoxins bind specifically to toxin molecules, neutralising them so they can no longer harm the body's cells.

questions.q: At a synapse, transmission is unidirectional because:
options: Calcium ions only enter the postsynaptic neurone
Neurotransmitter receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane and vesicles only on the presynaptic side
Acetylcholinesterase is found only presynaptically
The synaptic cleft is too wide for diffusion
questions.explain: Vesicles releasing neurotransmitter are confined to the presynaptic neurone and receptors to the postsynaptic membrane, so signals pass one way.

questions.q: During atrial systole, blood moves from the atria into the ventricles because:
options: Atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure, pushing the AV valves open
The semilunar valves open
The atria relax and fill with blood
Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
questions.explain: Contraction of the atria raises atrial pressure above that of the ventricles, forcing the open AV valves to allow blood through.

questions.q: During the refractory period immediately after an action potential, a second impulse cannot be generated because:
options: The potassium channels are permanently open
Myelin temporarily disappears
Calcium ions block the axon
The sodium channels are inactivated and the membrane is recovering its resting state
questions.explain: Inactivated Na+ channels and ongoing repolarisation mean the membrane cannot fire again, ensuring discrete, one-way impulses.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: The secondary immune response is faster and stronger than the primary because:
options: Phagocytosis no longer occurs
The pathogen has fewer antigens
Memory cells rapidly divide and differentiate into plasma cells, producing antibodies quickly
Antigens are weaker on second exposure
questions.explain: Memory cells formed during the primary response allow a rapid proliferation of plasma cells and a higher, quicker antibody output.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: When the body overheats, heat loss is increased by:
options: Vasodilation of skin arterioles and increased sweating
Raising of body hairs
Constriction of skin arterioles
Shivering of skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Vasodilation brings more warm blood to the skin surface and sweating removes heat by evaporation, both increasing heat loss.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic (killer) T-cells destroy infected body cells by:
options: Secreting antibodies that agglutinate them
Engulfing them by phagocytosis
Stimulating B-cells to divide
Releasing perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane so the cell dies
questions.explain: Cytotoxic T-cells release perforin that perforates the membrane of infected cells, causing them to die before the pathogen can multiply.

questions.q: In a fish gill, the counter-current flow of water and blood is efficient because:
options: Blood and water flow in the same direction, equalising oxygen quickly
A diffusion gradient for oxygen is maintained across the entire length of the lamella
Water flows faster than blood, reversing the gradient
It allows carbon dioxide to be reabsorbed into the blood
questions.explain: Counter-current flow keeps the oxygen concentration of water higher than that of blood along the whole gill lamella, maintaining a diffusion gradient throughout.

questions.q: How is the magnitude (intensity) of a stimulus conveyed to the central nervous system?
options: By the size of each action potential
By the frequency of action potentials and the number of neurones firing
By the speed of the action potential
By the duration of the resting potential
questions.explain: Because action potentials are all-or-nothing, a stronger stimulus is signalled by a higher firing frequency and recruitment of more neurones.

questions.q: When a B-cell is activated and divides, the process that produces many identical cells is called:
options: Reverse transcription
Clonal expansion (clonal selection)
Agglutination
Antigenic variation
questions.explain: The selected B-cell divides by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells, some becoming plasma cells and others memory cells.

questions.q: HIV is described as a retrovirus because it:
options: Has no genetic material
Reproduces only outside cells
Lacks a protein coat
Contains RNA and uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA inside the host cell
questions.explain: HIV carries RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which produces DNA from the viral RNA so it can integrate into the host genome.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
They destroy all the host's T-cells
They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: On a cold day, the body conserves heat by:
options: Vasodilation of skin arterioles
Increased sweating
Relaxation of erector pili muscles
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, reducing blood flow to the surface
questions.explain: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface, decreasing heat loss by radiation.

questions.q: The ELISA test uses antibodies linked to an enzyme to:
options: Destroy a pathogen in a sample
Vaccinate a patient against a disease
Detect the presence of a specific antigen or antibody by producing a colour change
Replace a missing hormone
questions.explain: In an ELISA, an enzyme-linked antibody binds its target and the enzyme then catalyses a colour change, revealing presence and amount.

questions.q: Bacteria and viruses are examples of pathogens. A key difference relevant to immunity is that viruses:
options: Can only reproduce inside a host cell using its machinery
Are killed by most antibiotics
Have a peptidoglycan cell wall
Are larger than bacteria
questions.explain: Viruses are intracellular parasites that hijack host-cell machinery to replicate, which is why they evade antibiotics.
